claim: 76 ecologically diverse wild yeast isolates were analyzed in this study.
source: Here, we analyzed 76 ecologically diverse wild yeast isolates and discovered a wide diversity of replicative lifespan (RLS).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of isolates analyzed.

claim: The study discovered a wide diversity of replicative lifespan (RLS) among the wild yeast isolates.
source: Here, we analyzed 76 ecologically diverse wild yeast isolates and discovered a wide diversity of replicative lifespan (RLS).
evidence: The manuscript states this as a finding from the analysis.

claim: The collection included 40 diploid isolates of Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source: This collection included 40 diploid isolates of Saccharomyces cerevisiae and 36 diploid isolates of Saccharomyces paradoxus (Hyma and Fay, 2013; Liti et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the composition of the strain collection with citations.

claim: The collection included 36 diploid isolates of Saccharomyces paradoxus.
source: This collection included 40 diploid isolates of Saccharomyces cerevisiae and 36 diploid isolates of Saccharomyces paradoxus (Hyma and Fay, 2013; Liti et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the composition of the strain collection with citations.

claim: S. cerevisiae and S. paradoxus share a common ancestor between 0.4 and 3 million years ago.
source: S. cerevisiae and S. paradoxus are closely related (share a common ancestor between 0.4 and 3 million years ago), with 90% genome identity, and can mate and produce viable progeny (Liti et al., 2006; Tirosh et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature for this evolutionary relationship.

claim: S. cerevisiae and S. paradoxus have 90% genome identity.
source: S. cerevisiae and S. paradoxus are closely related (share a common ancestor between 0.4 and 3 million years ago), with 90% genome identity, and can mate and produce viable progeny (Liti et al., 2006; Tirosh et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature for this genomic similarity.

claim: S. cerevisiae and S. paradoxus can mate and produce viable progeny.
source: S. cerevisiae and S. paradoxus are closely related (share a common ancestor between 0.4 and 3 million years ago), with 90% genome identity, and can mate and produce viable progeny (Liti et al., 2006; Tirosh et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature for this reproductive compatibility.

claim: Most wild isolates grew faster than the diploid laboratory wild-type BY4743 strain under both YPD and YPG conditions.
source: Most wild isolates grew faster than the diploid laboratory wild-type (WT) BY4743 strain under both conditions, with an average doubling time of 65 min in YPD and 125 min in YPG (Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports measured doubling times and references Figure 1A.

claim: The average doubling time of wild isolates was 65 min in YPD.
source: Most wild isolates grew faster than the diploid laboratory wild-type (WT) BY4743 strain under both conditions, with an average doubling time of 65 min in YPD and 125 min in YPG (Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports measured doubling times.

claim: The average doubling time of wild isolates was 125 min in YPG.
source: Most wild isolates grew faster than the diploid laboratory wild-type (WT) BY4743 strain under both conditions, with an average doubling time of 65 min in YPD and 125 min in YPG (Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports measured doubling times.

claim: A ~10-fold variation in median and maximum RLS was observed across the isolates under YPD condition.
source: Under the YPD condition, we observed a remarkable ~10-fold variation in median and maximum RLS (Pearson correlation coefficient = 0.65 between median and maximum RLS, p < 0.00001) across these isolates (Figure 1B, C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the observed variation with statistical analysis.

claim: There is a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.65 between median and maximum RLS (p < 0.00001).
source: Under the YPD condition, we observed a remarkable ~10-fold variation in median and maximum RLS (Pearson correlation coefficient = 0.65 between median and maximum RLS, p < 0.00001) across these isolates (Figure 1B, C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the statistical correlation between lifespan measures.

claim: The average median RLS of S. paradoxus strains (29.7) was significantly higher (p = 2.7 × 10−9) than the average median RLS of S. cerevisiae strains (22.7).
source: The average median RLS of S. paradoxus strains (29.7) was significantly higher (p = 2.7 × 10−9) than the average median RLS of S. cerevisiae strains (22.7) (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript reports measured RLS values with statistical significance.

claim: S. paradoxus strain Y7 showed the longest median RLS (RLS = 42).
source: Among the 76 strains analyzed, S. paradoxus strain Y7 showed the longest median RLS (RLS = 42), whereas S. cerevisiae strain Y10 exhibited the shortest median RLS, with 50 % of Y10 cells ceasing division after producing only four daughters (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the measured RLS for specific strains.

claim: S. cerevisiae strain Y10 exhibited the shortest median RLS, with 50% of Y10 cells ceasing division after producing only four daughters.
source: Among the 76 strains analyzed, S. paradoxus strain Y7 showed the longest median RLS (RLS = 42), whereas S. cerevisiae strain Y10 exhibited the shortest median RLS, with 50 % of Y10 cells ceasing division after producing only four daughters (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the measured RLS for specific strains.

claim: Glycerol as a growth substrate can extend both RLS and chronological lifespan (CLS).
source: Glycerol as a growth substrate can extend both RLS and chronological lifespan (CLS; Burtner et al., 2009; Kaeberlein et al., 2005a).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature for this effect.

claim: 32 strains showed significant (p < 0.05) median RLS increase on YPG.
source: While we observed a significant (p < 0.05, Wilcoxon rank sum test) median RLS increase in 32 strains on YPG with 24 strains significantly decreased median RLS; and the remaining 7 strains showed no significant changes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of strains with significant changes.

claim: 24 strains showed significantly decreased median RLS on YPG.
source: While we observed a significant (p < 0.05, Wilcoxon rank sum test) median RLS increase in 32 strains on YPG with 24 strains significantly decreased median RLS; and the remaining 7 strains showed no significant changes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of strains with significant changes.

claim: 7 strains showed no significant changes in median RLS on YPG.
source: While we observed a significant (p < 0.05, Wilcoxon rank sum test) median RLS increase in 32 strains on YPG with 24 strains significantly decreased median RLS; and the remaining 7 strains showed no significant changes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of strains with no significant changes.

claim: Strains with the shortest RLS on YPD tended to achieve the longest lifespans on YPG.
source: Interestingly, strains with the shortest RLS on YPD tended to achieve the longest lifespans on YPG, while the long-lived strains on YPD generally did not show a further RLS increase (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C) (Pearson correlation coefficient = −0.51 between median RLS on YPD and median RLS on YPG, p < 0.0001).
evidence: The manuscript reports the observed pattern with statistical correlation.

claim: There is a Pearson correlation coefficient of −0.51 between median RLS on YPD and median RLS on YPG (p < 0.0001).
source: Interestingly, strains with the shortest RLS on YPD tended to achieve the longest lifespans on YPG, while the long-lived strains on YPD generally did not show a further RLS increase (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C) (Pearson correlation coefficient = −0.51 between median RLS on YPD and median RLS on YPG, p < 0.0001).
evidence: The manuscript reports the statistical correlation.

claim: ≥5 million 150 bp paired-end RNA-seq reads were obtained for each strain grown on YPD.
source: In the case of the transcriptome, we obtained ≥5 million 150 bp paired-end RNA-seq reads for each strain grown on YPD.
evidence: The manuscript reports the sequencing depth.

claim: The dataset contained RNA-seq reads for 5376 genes commonly across all isolates.
source: After filtering and quality control, the dataset contained RNA-seq reads for 5376 genes and 166 metabolites identified commonly across all isolates (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of genes after filtering.

claim: The dataset contained 166 metabolites identified commonly across all isolates.
source: After filtering and quality control, the dataset contained RNA-seq reads for 5376 genes and 166 metabolites identified commonly across all isolates (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of metabolites after filtering.

claim: The expression profiles between strains were similar to one another, with Spearman correlation coefficients of strain pairs ranging between 0.59 and 0.93.
source: The expression profiles between strains were similar to one another, with Spearman correlation coefficients of strain pairs ranging between 0.59 and 0.93 (except the pairing involving Q59.1, CBS5829, YPS606, and UFRJ50791, with the range between 0.21 and 0.79) (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports the correlation analysis results.

claim: 73 transcripts showed significant correlation with median RLS (padj ≤ 0.01; 39 with positive correlation and 34 with negative correlation).
source: With the PGLS approach, we identified 73 transcripts with significant correlation with median RLS (padj ≤ 0.01; 39 with positive correlation and 34 with negative correlation) (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of the PGLS analysis.

claim: CMR3 (putative zinc finger protein coding gene) showed positive correlation with RLS (padj = 3.3 × 10−9).
source: Among the top hits with positive correlation were a putative zinc finger protein coding gene CMR3 (padj = 3.3 × 10−9), histone acetyltransferase (HAT) gene HPA2 (padj = 0.0002), transcription factor TEC1 (padj = 9.3 × 10−6), and zing regulated protein gene ZRG8 (padj = 0.006) (Figure 3A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports the statistical significance of the correlation.

claim: HPA2 (histone acetyltransferase gene) showed positive correlation with RLS (padj = 0.0002).
source: Among the top hits with positive correlation were a putative zinc finger protein coding gene CMR3 (padj = 3.3 × 10−9), histone acetyltransferase (HAT) gene HPA2 (padj = 0.0002), transcription factor TEC1 (padj = 9.3 × 10−6), and zing regulated protein gene ZRG8 (padj = 0.006) (Figure 3A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports the statistical significance of the correlation.

claim: TEC1 (transcription factor) showed positive correlation with RLS (padj = 9.3 × 10−6).
source: Among the top hits with positive correlation were a putative zinc finger protein coding gene CMR3 (padj = 3.3 × 10−9), histone acetyltransferase (HAT) gene HPA2 (padj = 0.0002), transcription factor TEC1 (padj = 9.3 × 10−6), and zing regulated protein gene ZRG8 (padj = 0.006) (Figure 3A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports the statistical significance of the correlation.

claim: ZRG8 (zinc regulated protein gene) showed positive correlation with RLS (padj = 0.006).
source: Among the top hits with positive correlation were a putative zinc finger protein coding gene CMR3 (padj = 3.3 × 10−9), histone acetyltransferase (HAT) gene HPA2 (padj = 0.0002), transcription factor TEC1 (padj = 9.3 × 10−6), and zing regulated protein gene ZRG8 (padj = 0.006) (Figure 3A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports the statistical significance of the correlation.

claim: PCL1 (cyclin-dependent kinase Pho85p interacting protein) showed negative correlation with RLS (padj = 0.0008).
source: The top hits with negative correlation included the genes coding for cyclin-dependent kinase Pho85p interacting proteins PCL1 (padj = 0.0008) and PCL2 (padj = 0.001), regulator of Ty1 transposon protein coding gene RTT107 (padj = 0.007), and inositol monophosphatase gene INM1 (padj = 0.006) (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports the statistical significance of the correlation.

claim: PCL2 (cyclin-dependent kinase Pho85p interacting protein) showed negative correlation with RLS (padj = 0.001).
source: The top hits with negative correlation included the genes coding for cyclin-dependent kinase Pho85p interacting proteins PCL1 (padj = 0.0008) and PCL2 (padj = 0.001), regulator of Ty1 transposon protein coding gene RTT107 (padj = 0.007), and inositol monophosphatase gene INM1 (padj = 0.006) (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports the statistical significance of the correlation.

claim: RTT107 (regulator of Ty1 transposon protein coding gene) showed negative correlation with RLS (padj = 0.007).
source: The top hits with negative correlation included the genes coding for cyclin-dependent kinase Pho85p interacting proteins PCL1 (padj = 0.0008) and PCL2 (padj = 0.001), regulator of Ty1 transposon protein coding gene RTT107 (padj = 0.007), and inositol monophosphatase gene INM1 (padj = 0.006) (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports the statistical significance of the correlation.

claim: INM1 (inositol monophosphatase gene) showed negative correlation with RLS (padj = 0.006).
source: The top hits with negative correlation included the genes coding for cyclin-dependent kinase Pho85p interacting proteins PCL1 (padj = 0.0008) and PCL2 (padj = 0.001), regulator of Ty1 transposon protein coding gene RTT107 (padj = 0.007), and inositol monophosphatase gene INM1 (padj = 0.006) (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports the statistical significance of the correlation.

claim: GenAge identifies 611 genes from the published literature with effects on RLS.
source: GenAge identifies 611 genes from the published literature with effects on RLS (decreased or increased) of laboratory yeast strains (595 deletion mutants and 16 overexpressed genes) (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The manuscript cites the GenAge database content.

claim: Of 5376 genes whose expression was measured across the wild isolates, there were 39 genes present in both the study's list and GenAge.
source: Of 5376 genes whose expression was measured across the wild isolates, there were 39 genes present in both our list and GenAge, 23 of which showed the same direction of correlation with RLS.
evidence: The manuscript reports the overlap analysis results.

claim: 23 of the 39 overlapping genes showed the same direction of correlation with RLS.
source: Of 5376 genes whose expression was measured across the wild isolates, there were 39 genes present in both our list and GenAge, 23 of which showed the same direction of correlation with RLS.
evidence: The manuscript reports the overlap analysis results.

claim: 31 metabolites exhibited significant association with median RLS (padj ≤ 0.05).
source: Among 166 metabolites that we examined, 31 exhibited significant association with median RLS (padj ≤ 0.05) (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of the metabolite analysis.

claim: Tryptophan correlated positively with RLS.
source: Among the top hits, tryptophan, lactate, 2-hydroxyglutarate, 3-hydroxypropionic acid, 2-hydroxyisobutyrate, 2-hydroxybutyrate, and phenyl-lactic acid (PLA) correlated positively (Figure 5A), whereas lysine, quinolinic acid (QA), propionate, Se-methylselenocysteine showed negative correlation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the correlation results.

claim: Lactate correlated positively with RLS.
source: Among the top hits, tryptophan, lactate, 2-hydroxyglutarate, 3-hydroxypropionic acid, 2-hydroxyisobutyrate, 2-hydroxybutyrate, and phenyl-lactic acid (PLA) correlated positively (Figure 5A), whereas lysine, quinolinic acid (QA), propionate, Se-methylselenocysteine showed negative correlation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the correlation results.

claim: Lysine correlated negatively with RLS.
source: Among the top hits, tryptophan, lactate, 2-hydroxyglutarate, 3-hydroxypropionic acid, 2-hydroxyisobutyrate, 2-hydroxybutyrate, and phenyl-lactic acid (PLA) correlated positively (Figure 5A), whereas lysine, quinolinic acid (QA), propionate, Se-methylselenocysteine showed negative correlation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the correlation results.

claim: Quinolinic acid (QA) correlated negatively with RLS.
source: Among the top hits, tryptophan, lactate, 2-hydroxyglutarate, 3-hydroxypropionic acid, 2-hydroxyisobutyrate, 2-hydroxybutyrate, and phenyl-lactic acid (PLA) correlated positively (Figure 5A), whereas lysine, quinolinic acid (QA), propionate, Se-methylselenocysteine showed negative correlation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the correlation results.

claim: BNA2 gene expression was significantly downregulated (padj = 0.02) in long-lived wild isolates.
source: Further evidence for metabolic regulation of Trp in long-lived strains came from our transcriptome data wherein BNA2 (indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase) gene, which supports the first rate-limiting step of Trp catabolism (Pinson et al., 2019), was significantly downregulated (padj = 0.02) in long-lived wild isolates (Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript reports the statistical significance of the gene expression change.

claim: There is a significant positive correlation (R = 0.28, padj = 0.016) between OCR and median RLS.
source: Our analysis revealed a significant positive correlation (R = 0.28, padj = 0.016) between OCR and median RLS (Figure 6—figure supplement 4A, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports the statistical correlation between respiration and lifespan.

claim: Increased expression of BNA2 caused a significant decrease in median RLS in two out of three long-lived strains tested.
source: Consistent with the findings from transcriptomic data, the increased expression of BNA2 caused a significant decrease in median RLS in two out of three long-lived strains tested and significantly decreased maximum RLS in all long-lived strains tested (Figure 7A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the experimental results.

claim: Increased expression of BNA2 significantly decreased maximum RLS in all long-lived strains tested.
source: Consistent with the findings from transcriptomic data, the increased expression of BNA2 caused a significant decrease in median RLS in two out of three long-lived strains tested and significantly decreased maximum RLS in all long-lived strains tested (Figure 7A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the experimental results.

claim: GLN1 overexpression significantly decreased both median and maximum RLS of long-lived strains tested.
source: We found that GLN1 overexpression significantly decreased both median and maximum RLS of long-lived strains tested (Wilcoxon rank sum tests, p < 0.05) (Figure 7A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the experimental results with statistical significance.

claim: Elimination of mtDNA abolished the growth ability of long-lived strains in the medium supplemented with α-KG as a sole carbon source.
source: We found that elimination of mtDNA in long-lived strains abolished their growth ability in the medium supplemented with α-KG as a sole carbon source (Figure 8A).
evidence: The manuscript reports the experimental results.

claim: The loss of mtDNA caused a significant reduction in RLS in all three strains tested.
source: Our analysis revealed that the loss of mtDNA caused a significant reduction in RLS in all three strains tested (Wilcoxon rank sum tests, p < 0.05) (Figure 8B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the experimental results with statistical significance.

claim: The Greenland shark (Somniosus microcephalus) may live for more than 500 years.
source: Across eukaryotic species, longevity can differ over many orders of magnitude, from days to centuries, for example the Greenland shark (Somniosus microcephalus) may live for more than 500 years whereas some species live only several days (Mortimer and Johnston, 1959; Nielsen et al., 2016; Jones et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature for this lifespan example.

claim: Longevity varies among individuals of the same species.
source: Longevity also varies among individuals of the same species, indicating that variability of lifespan is not constrained at the level of species, and that the molecular determinants of lifespan vary within the same genetic pool (Finch and Pike, 1996; Klass, 1983; Kaya et al., 2015; Ma et al., 2018; Dato et al., 2018; Wright et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature for this observation.

claim: Artificially created mutant strains may show longer lifespan under laboratory settings but demonstrate reduced fitness in their natural environment.
source: For example, artificially created mutant strains may show longer lifespan under laboratory settings but demonstrate reduced fitness in their natural environment (Bartke et al., 2001; Jenkins et al., 2004; Chen et al., 2007; Delaney et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature for this observation.

claim: Almost half of the strains have mosaic recombinant genomes arising from outcrosses between genetically distinct lineages of the same species.
source: Based on these studies, it was shown that while some of these strains fall into distinct lineages with unique genetic variants, almost half of the strains have mosaic recombinant genomes arising from outcrosses between genetically distinct lineages of the same species (Liti et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature for this genomic observation.

claim: The first three principal components explain ~49% of total variance in gene expression.
source: PCA of the transcriptome revealed a pattern resembling the phylogenetic relationship, with the first three principal components (PCs explaining ~49 % of total variance in gene expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A)).
evidence: The manuscript reports the PCA results.

claim: The first three PCs explain ~41% of total variance in metabolite levels.
source: PCA of metabolomics data revealed a similar structure with the first three PCs explaining ~41 % of total variance in metabolite levels, and PC2 somewhat separating the species (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The manuscript reports the PCA results.

claim: 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid, an intermediate from Trp degradation, can be used as a substrate to synthesize α-ketoadipate.
source: For example, it has been shown that 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid, an intermediate from Trp degradation, can be used as a substrate to synthesize α-ketoadipate (Hallen et al., 2013; Tobes and Mason, 1975), which is then converted by ARO8 to Lys (Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature for this metabolic pathway.

claim: The combined deletion of BNA2 and LYS20 or BNA2 with LYS21 causes synthetic lethality.
source: In addition, at the genetic level, while individual KO lines of BNA2, LYS20, or LYS21 are not lethal, it was found that the combined deletion of BNA2 and LYS20 or BNA2 with LYS21 causes synthetic lethality (Deutscher et al., 2006), possibly by causing Lys auxotrophy.
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature for this genetic interaction.

claim: Yeast produces PLA through a nonspecific activity of lactate dehydrogenase from phenylpyruvate.
source: Previously, it was found that yeast produces PLA through a nonspecific activity of lactate dehydrogenase from phenylpyruvate, a metabolite derived from chorismate in the shikimate pathway (Srinivasan and Smolke, 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature for this metabolic pathway.

claim: Glycolytic genes such as FBA1, TDH2, PGK1, ENO2, and CDC19 were negatively correlated with RLS.
source: For example, we found that glycolytic genes such as FBA1, TDH2, PGK1, ENO2, and CDC19 were negatively correlated with RLS, while TCA cycle genes such as CIT1, IDP1, and KGD1 were positively correlated with RLS (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports the correlation analysis results.

claim: TCA cycle genes such as CIT1, IDP1, and KGD1 were positively correlated with RLS.
source: For example, we found that glycolytic genes such as FBA1, TDH2, PGK1, ENO2, and CDC19 were negatively correlated with RLS, while TCA cycle genes such as CIT1, IDP1, and KGD1 were positively correlated with RLS (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports the correlation analysis results.

claim: Genetic induction of respiration in the PSY316 laboratory-adapted strain is sufficient to increase RLS.
source: This is also consistent with prior data that genetic induction of respiration in the PSY316 laboratory-adapted strain is sufficient to increase RLS (Lin et al., 2002).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature for this observation.

claim: Restriction of BCAAs was shown to increase both healthspan and longevity in mice.
source: For example, restriction of BCAAs was shown to increase both healthspan and longevity in mice (Wolfson et al., 2016; Richardson et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature for this dietary intervention effect.

claim: Reducing the amino acid content of the media can increase RLS in a short-lived laboratory yeast strain.
source: Jiang et al. first reported that reducing the amino acid content of the media can increase RLS in a short-lived laboratory yeast strain (Jiang et al., 2000).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature for this dietary effect.

claim: Asp restriction can extend RLS by inhibiting TOR.
source: Similarly, Asp restriction (Powers et al., 2006) or treatment with the glutamine synthetase inhibitor methionine sulfoximine (Kaeberlein et al., 2005b) can extend RLS by inhibiting TOR.
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature for this mechanism.

claim: A decrease in KYN metabolic pathway activity through RNAi knockdown of TDO-2 expression was found to robustly extend lifespan in C. elegans.
source: Recently, a decrease in KYN metabolic pathway activity through RNAi knockdown of TDO-2 (BNA2 ortholog) expression (knockdown) was found to robustly extend lifespan (van der Goot et al., 2012), while complete KO of TDO-2 expression diminished the positive lifespan effect in C. elegans (Michels et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature for this lifespan effect.

claim: Complete KO of TDO-2 expression diminished the positive lifespan effect in C. elegans.
source: Recently, a decrease in KYN metabolic pathway activity through RNAi knockdown of TDO-2 (BNA2 ortholog) expression (knockdown) was found to robustly extend lifespan (van der Goot et al., 2012), while complete KO of TDO-2 expression diminished the positive lifespan effect in C. elegans (Michels et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature for this lifespan effect.

claim: Increased KYN pathway activity and alteration in KYN pathway metabolites with age have been observed in humans.
source: Increased KYN pathway activity and alteration in KYN pathway metabolites with age have also been observed in humans, suggesting a possible conserved role for this pathway in lifespan regulation (de Bie et al., 2016; Chatterjee et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature for this observation in humans.

claim: A study across 26 mammalian species found that species characterized by increased KYN pathway activity were shorter lived.
source: In addition, a study across 26 mammalian species found that species characterized by increased KYN pathway activity were shorter lived (Powers et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature for this comparative study.

claim: Deletion of BNA2 decreased RLS in diploid laboratory WT cells.
source: In yeast, it was shown that deletion of BNA2, which encodes the protein that controls the first rate-limiting step in Trp catabolism, decreased RLS, while increased BNA2 dosage (overexpression) increased RLS in diploid laboratory WT cells (Beas et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature for this genetic effect.

claim: Increased BNA2 dosage (overexpression) increased RLS in diploid laboratory WT cells.
source: In yeast, it was shown that deletion of BNA2, which encodes the protein that controls the first rate-limiting step in Trp catabolism, decreased RLS, while increased BNA2 dosage (overexpression) increased RLS in diploid laboratory WT cells (Beas et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature for this genetic effect.

claim: Increased expression of PNC1 alone has been shown to modulate intracellular NAD+ homeostasis and to increase RLS.
source: Increased expression of PNC1 alone has been shown to modulate intracellular NAD+ homeostasis and to increase RLS (Beas et al., 2020; Choudhary et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature for this genetic effect.

claim: When NAD+ demand is higher relative to ATP turnover, cells engage in anaerobic glycolysis, despite available oxygen.
source: Previously, it has been shown in both yeast and mammalian cells that when NAD+ demand is higher relative to ATP turnover, cells engage in anaerobic glycolysis, despite available oxygen (Luengo et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature for this metabolic regulation.

claim: α-KG was shown to decrease ATP levels by blocking mitochondrial complex V activity in C. elegans.
source: In C. elegans, α-KG was found to decrease ATP levels by blocking mitochondrial complex V activity, thereby reducing oxygen consumption. This effect was found to be mTOR dependent (Chin et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature for this mechanism.

claim: α-KG was found to extend lifespan in fruit fly by inhibiting mTOR and activating AMPK signaling.
source: Similarly, α-KG was found to extend lifespan in fruit fly by inhibiting mTOR and activating AMPK signaling (Su et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature for this mechanism.

claim: In mid-aged mice, α-KG supplementation decreased systemic inflammatory cytokines leading to health and lifespan benefits.
source: In mid-aged mice, α-KG supplementation decreased systemic inflammatory cytokines leading to health and lifespan benefits (Asadi Shahmirzadi et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature for this intervention effect.

claim: An analysis of 178 genetically characterized inbred fly strains revealed α-KG-dependent lifespan regulation under dietary restricted conditions.
source: More recently, an analysis of 178 genetically characterized inbred fly strains revealed α-KG-dependent lifespan regulation under dietary restricted conditions (Jin et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature for this genetic analysis.

claim: Yeast can actively transport α-KG from medium to cytosol and into mitochondria.
source: It was shown that yeast can actively transport α-KG from medium to cytosol and into mitochondria (Casal et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature for this transport mechanism.

claim: α-KG supplementation was found to increase oxygen consumption in yeast.
source: In addition, in contrast with the findings in C. elegans, α-KG supplementation was found to increase oxygen consumption in yeast (Casal et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature for this metabolic effect.

claim: α-KG supplementation was shown to increase oxidative stress resistance in yeast.
source: Also, α-KG supplementation was shown to increase oxidative stress resistance in yeast (Bayliak et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature for this stress resistance effect.

claim: Glu restriction was found to increase yeast chronological lifespan (CLS).
source: Initially, Glu restriction was found to increase yeast chronological lifespan (CLS; Wu et al., 2013); however, later on, it was shown that Glu supplementation also has a positive effect on CLS (Powers et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature for this dietary effect.

claim: Glu supplementation has a positive effect on CLS in yeast.
source: Initially, Glu restriction was found to increase yeast chronological lifespan (CLS; Wu et al., 2013); however, later on, it was shown that Glu supplementation also has a positive effect on CLS (Powers et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature for this dietary effect.

claim: In C. elegans, medium supplemented with a lower dose (1–5 mM) of Glu was found to extend lifespan.
source: Similarly, in C. elegans, medium supplemented with a lower dose (1–5 mM) of Glu was found to extend lifespan (Canfield, 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature for this dietary effect.

claim: NH4 has been shown to be involved in regulation of mTOR1 and mTOR2 signaling.
source: Furthermore, catalysis of Glu to α-KG also yields NH4, which has been shown to be involved in regulation of mTOR1 and mTOR2 signaling (Tate and Cooper, 2003; Stracka et al., 2014) and lifespan.
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature for this signaling mechanism.

claim: Long-lived strains are characterized with decreased glycolytic activity and amino acid biosynthesis and increased mitochondrial activity.
source: In summary, our joint omics analyses revealed consistent changes associated with increased lifespan at both metabolome and transcriptome levels, pointing to decreased glycolytic activity and amino biosynthesis and increased mitochondrial activity (TCA cycle and mitochondrial respiration) even under conditions of excess fermentative carbon source (glucose).
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the integrated omics findings.

claim: Long-lived strains show decreased Trp degradation through the KYN pathway.
source: Our data highlight the importance of Trp metabolism in lifespan regulation in long-lived strains. We found that even though the Trp biosynthesis pathway (shikimate pathway) is suppressed, Trp levels were increased, possibly due to decreased transcript abundance of BNA2, which controls the first rate-limiting step in Trp degradation.
evidence: The manuscript infers this mechanism from the combined metabolite and transcript data.

claim: Decreased amino acid biosynthesis in long-lived strains may spare glutamate for conversion to α-KG to fuel the TCA cycle.
source: We hypothesize that compartment-specific glutamate (Glu) to α-KG flux, a reaction mainly controlled by NAD+-dependent mitochondrial Glu dehydrogenase, GDH2 in mitochondria (Han et al., 2019; Sickmann et al., 2003; Mara et al., 2018), might support increased TCA activity. In this case, spared Glu (due to decreased Glu-dependent amino acid biosynthesis) can support citrate synthesis to fuel TCA cycle via α-KG conversion.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this hypothesis based on the observed metabolic patterns.

claim: Increased NADH levels in long-lived strains might be due to increased NAD+-dependent GDH2 activity.
source: Although it needs additional experimental evidence, we think that increased nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) + hydrogen (H) (NADH) levels in long-lived strains might be due to increased NAD+-dependent GDH2 activity, which catalyzes the conversion of Glu to α-KG in mitochondria.
evidence: The manuscript speculates on this mechanism based on the observed patterns.

claim: Many wild yeast isolates can utilize α-KG as an alternative carbon source for growth.
source: Here, we also showed that wild yeast isolates can use α-KG as an alternative carbon source for growth.
evidence: The manuscript reports this experimental finding.

claim: The genetic architecture of trait variation in natural populations may differ from that assumed from studies of lab strains.
source: It is also possible that the genetic architecture of trait variation in natural populations may differ from that which is assumed from studies of lab strains, including extensive single-gene studies of lifespan variation in yeast (McCormick et al., 2015). The lack of overlap between the genes whose expression correlates with lifespan variation in wild isolates and genes that affect RLS in single-mutant studies on laboratory WT background supports this possibility.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the lack of overlap between wild isolate and lab strain results.
